The flag only names what the old builder hard-coded, the Store’s data does not change, and the owner’s pre-release decision on opengwas/opengwasdb#298 applies such metadata changes in place (#359 relabels the manifests). So the amendment check tolerates exactly one difference: a recorded argv that names no --association-coverage matches a planned argv that differs by the declaration-derived pair alone. A record that names a coverage – another value included – is compared whole, as is every other token, and the bundle’s manifest membership is still compared byte for byte. title: Association Coverage is declared in the Release Bundle, in one vocabulary
text:
Every committed bundle declares its true coverage; pixi run bundle-check requires it and OGS-00006 says signals_only.
The amendment check tolerates that one difference and nothing else (see above), so a published Ragged Store whose build record predates the flag will gain its own completion without a rebuild once single-id Ragged completion lands. That layout is still refused today, by SINGLE_ID_COMPLETION_LAYOUTS in src/ogstores/plan.py; lifting the gate is #336 in epic #232.
Manifest Generation requires association_coverage in every release config, writes it after label: in the candidate release.yaml, and refuses a config without one. For a region-filtered config it must equal region_policy.association_coverage exactly: a release config and a bundle take only the four current values, and canonical_association_coverage is only for reading frozen historical evidence.
The Analysis Catalog reads release.yaml for stores.association_coverage, the coverage count dimension and the summary report; it no longer reads the Validation Record’s observed.association_coverage, which stays the value opengwasdb reports (ADR 0039 is amended accordingly).
docs/spec/release-config.md, docs/spec/analysis-catalog.md, docs/release-metadata-schema.md and CONTEXT.md’s Association Coverage entry state the four values.

Amends ADR 0029. association_coverage is restored to release.yaml; the other nine keys ADR 0029 removed stay removed, and its reasons for removing them are untouched.

title: One home per kind of thing
text:
The repository grew three homes for Python and a fourth for everything else. Reviewing #299, the user asked why /curation, /resources and /src all exist. Decided on 21 Oct 2026 (#317):

Python lived in three places. The two workflows’ packages were under src/ (#249). The curation package sat at the repository root, and the command-line tools that check bundles, audit Indexed Variant Subsets and render the readiness view were loose scripts in resources/scripts/.
resources/scripts/ contradicted “resources/ is inputs”. It held the test runner, the bundle check, the site build and its report sources, benchmarks, GWAS Catalog and OpenGWAS acquisition scripts, and one reviewed input, the dbGaP key-discrepancy ledger. CONTRIBUTING called it “the one directory at risk of becoming a junk drawer”, and asked people to move things out when they became steps. That rule is a judgement, so no test could check it.
Reference Resources kept their build scripts beside their data, and the SomaScan target generators sat with the Manifest Generators.



Each kind of thing has one home, and a test checks it.
stores/            output: Release Bundles; stores.tsv and STORES.md beside it
src/               all importable Python
  ogstores/          Store Release Build and the Release Bundle contract, with the
                     readiness and indexed-subset audit CLIs
  manifest_generation/  the shared pipeline and providers/, with the check_bundles CLI;
                     a provider's acquisition scripts, in any language, under it
  curation/          trait-mapping curation
workflow/          Snakemake wiring, and the release entry point
resources/         inputs only: reference-resources/, annotations/, inventories/,
                   generators/ (release configs, reviewed tables and receipts)
tools/             repository tooling that is neither a package nor an input
tests/             the suites, and run_all_tests.py
docs/              adr/, spec/, reports/ (report sources), and the rendered site
.github/           CI
To place a file, ask what it is: 1. Something the repository produces goes in stores/, or in docs/ if it is a report. 2. Something a workflow reads as data goes in resources/. That covers a release config, a reviewed table, a frozen inventory and a Reference Resource declaration. 3. Code a workflow imports or runs goes in src/. Python is a package module, run with python3 -m. A Source Provider’s acquisition script, in any language, goes in its providers/<provider>/. 4. A test or the test runner goes in tests/, and a report source in docs/reports/. Anything else a person runs, to maintain the repository or to build a Reference Resource, goes in tools/.
Three rules keep it true: - A CLI belongs with what it applies. Store Release Build imports nothing from Manifest Generation (ADR 0035). So the bundle check, which applies Manifest Generation’s rules as well as the contract, lives in manifest_generation, though what it checks is a Release Bundle. - Moving a file never breaks a path generation still reads. Those paths are frozen inventory provenance, the originals named there, and config inputs. A move that would break one re-freezes under a new snapshot id, or the file stays where it is. - An input whose content is unchanged may instead move with its recorded path, and the provenance pin that covers it, updated in place under the same snapshot id. This was decided for ukb-b’s declared selection (#252), so as not to disrupt the work that uses that inventory. - Any change to an input’s content still needs a new snapshot id. - Paths recorded in stores/ and in generation-*.yaml receipts are history and are never edited. So is a lineage string that records which tool changed a file, and so are the commands in a locked or preregistered record, such as the QC Panel Concordance Study’s preregistration. - tests/packaging/test_layout.py enforces the layout. - Python lives only in src/, tests/, tools/ and workflow/. None sits at the repository root, and none hides elsewhere as a namespace package such as rogue/module.py. - Only src/ and tests/ hold packages. - Nothing under resources/ is code. Clarified by #350: the exception for the legacy R generators retired with them, the last two being the metadata resolvers curation’s round-trip proof drove. The allow-list is gone, so the rule is now the code’s and not the list’s: resources/ holds no code at all. - resources/scripts/ does not come back.




Keep resources/scripts/ with a stricter README rule. The rule already existed, and the directory grew anyway. A guard needs a definition it can test, and “no code under resources/” is one.
Make every tool a package module. The LD-panel toolchain, the site build and the benchmarks are imported by nothing, and one benchmark deliberately imports another checkout’s opengwasdb. Packaging them adds install surface and has no consumer.
Move the legacy R generators too. Stage 2 of epic #282 deletes them (#288, #289), and their recorded commands and receipts resolve under resources/generators/. Moving them now would break those paths for code that is about to go.
Call the tooling directory scripts/. That names the form, not the kind, and it is what resources/scripts/ was.





curation/ is src/curation/. resources/scripts/ is gone, and each item has moved to the home above. The Reference Resource build and verify scripts and the SomaScan target generators are in tools/reference-resources/<resource>/.
GWAS Catalog’s sample-size resolver (gwas_catalog_ssf.R) and the resolver contract it sources (contract.R) moved beside ebi-studies.r in providers/gwas_catalog/: they are live GWAS Catalog code, and no ticket retires them. The legacy FinnGen and OpenGWAS resolvers source contract.R from there until #288 and #289 retire them.
Nothing was re-frozen. The only moved file named in frozen provenance is materialise-gwas-ssf-ragged.R, in the Chen 2023 inventory’s reformat_tool lineage. Generation reads that field as text and never resolves it.
An existing checkout picks up the new package location on its next pixi run, because pixi re-installs the editable package when pyproject.toml changes.
#252, in the same pull request, retired families/ and .rebuild133/.
ADR 0011 stands. Reference Resources are build inputs. Only their build scripts moved, to tools/.

title: Manifest Generation is one pipeline fed by source connectors
text:
Every Source Collection has its own end-to-end Manifest Generator today. They share only the end of the work: the Release Bundle contract, Manifest Generation’s rules and the emitter (#248, #250). Everything before that is written again per source: - Source Inventory reconciliation: GWAS Catalog uses the shared module, ukb-b has its own 1,100-line copy, and FinnGen does it in R; - driving opengwasdb resolve-analyses: GWAS Catalog and dbGaP each wrap it their own way, ukb-b uses a recorded resolution, and the R generators skip it; - ancestry and effect-scale estimation, done in R (ancestry.R, effect_scale_validation.R) against ADR 0017; - rendering the bundle files.
So a new data source costs a new generator. Many more sources are coming: more GWAS Catalog collections like Chen 2023 and Sun 2018, later FinnGen rounds, and dbGaP datasets that each look different. Decided in a design session for #249 on 15 Oct 2026.


Manifest Generation is one shared pipeline. A source plugs in through files, never through code the pipeline calls.
A source supplies four things:








Connector
Written per
What it produces




Acquisition
Source Provider (per Source Collection when the provider is inconsistent, as dbGaP is)
the files, and an Acquisition Manifest: location, size and checksum per file


Metadata adapter, in any language
the same
a Source Metadata Table: canonical per-Analysis source metadata, whose rows are the intended membership


Column Map
Source Collection
how OpenGWASDB’s generic tabular reader reads the collection’s files: columns and conventions


Release config
Store Release
identity, Selection, Build Recipe shape, Quality Check overrides



The pipeline does the rest, the same way for every source: 1. Freeze. Reconcile the selected intent against the Acquisition Manifest into a frozen Source Inventory. An intended Analysis with no file, a file nobody claims, or a duplicate fails the run.
Clarified by #283: “no file” means no Acquisition Manifest row at all. A row whose readiness status records why acquisition could not produce a usable file is an explained absence: the Analysis stays in the Source Inventory as a non-ready row and never becomes a release member. Freeze writes the selected rows of both connector files beside the inventory and checksums them into its provenance (spec). 2. Preflight. 3. Analysis Resolution of every Analysis, by OpenGWASDB. 4. Verify the records. 5. Trait Ontology Mapping, filling gaps from the Canonical Trait Mapping Table. 6. Release policy. Quality Checks, the Assigned Ancestry check, and the Store Composition Rule. 7. Render, check and emit.
The rules that make this hold:

Every Analysis is resolved; there is no declared-only path. A Source Format OpenGWASDB cannot resolve is a gap in OpenGWASDB. Its collections wait for OpenGWASDB rather than entering a bundle on the source’s claims. eQTLGen’s BESD waits for BESD resolution support.
OpenGWASDB measures and Manifest Generation decides. A Quality Check tests one Resolution Record measurement against a threshold. The shared default can be overridden per release, and the override is recorded. Each check is declared as an exclusion (an exclude_from_build audit row with its reason) or a warning. Every Analysis’s measurements are recorded whether it passes or not.
Clarified by #285: a check’s measurement comes from the Resolution Record, except where OpenGWASDB does not yet measure it. Today the only exception is effect-placeholder rows, read from a reviewed listing until core counts them. The Assigned Ancestry check of step 6 is itself a Quality Check (assigned_ancestry), as the Selection rule below requires.
Connectors are files, frozen with the inventory. Generation reads no live source. A metadata change is a reviewed re-freeze, never a silent difference between two runs.
Clarified by #347: shared code reads canonical connector columns only; it opens no source’s own metadata files. A source’s adapter reads them and writes facts into the Source Metadata Table: genotyping_technology (;-joined, source order, blank when unrecorded) and source_genome_build for the GWAS Catalog’s -meta.yaml sidecars. Which technologies are exempt from the MAF floor stays release policy over that fact column, and preflight’s build check compares source_genome_build with the release default, opening no sidecar. The GWAS Catalog’s download-pass columns and overlay live in its Acquisition Manifest writer, their only caller. A boundary test (tests/packaging/test_per_source_metadata.py) fails if shared code reads provider metadata again.
One Selection gives one Release Bundle. A collection split into several Store Releases is several Selections. Assigned Ancestry never moves an Analysis into another Store Release; a disagreement with the Selection is a Quality Check.
Clarified by #287: a source with no allele frequencies, such as Sun 2018, is still resolved. When its Resolution Record shows ancestry unmeasurable for that reason – under a MAF request, every row read counted without a frequency (maf_rows_missing equal to canonical_rows_observed), and no ancestry site – a release config may opt in (release_policy.trust_source_ancestry_without_af) to take the Source Metadata Table’s source_superpopulation as Assigned Ancestry, with Ancestry Assignment Method source_trusted_no_af. Each such Analysis is a warning-level assigned_ancestry Quality Check result, in validation.yaml and the Quality Check sidecar. Without the opt-in it is excluded as ancestry_unassigned. A measured ancestry never takes the source label, and a measured disagreement remains an exclusion; so does a source whose frequencies the fit could not read (palindromic sites only, unusable standard errors), which has frequencies rather than none.
Clarified by #290: a Selection may name no single super-population (release_policy.selection_superpopulation: multi-ancestry, dbGaP MVP’s META bucket, OGS-00016). Such a Selection never assigns Assigned Ancestry: each Analysis keeps its measured fit, recorded in the Quality Check sidecar and the ancestry sidecar, while the emitted Assigned Ancestry stays empty with Ancestry Assignment Method unassigned, exactly as the accepted MVP bundles carry it. The assigned_ancestry check is not_applicable there, so nothing is excluded for ancestry – not even a measured super-population, because the Selection claims none. And a release that names one may opt in (release_policy.keep_unassigned_ancestry_as_warning) to keep an Analysis the gates left unassigned, still unassigned, as a warning-level assigned_ancestry result in validation.yaml and the sidecar; a measured different super-population remains ancestry_not_eur, and without the opt-in nothing changes.
A Resolution Record belongs to the Analysis. It is kept once per Source Collection, keyed by the resolver’s fingerprint, and reused by every Selection. Each bundle’s resolution receipt names the records it used.
Tabular formats are data, not readers. A Column Map declares, for one Source Collection, the provider columns for each required and optional field and the collection’s conventions:

missing-value tokens;
effect type;
p-value form;
which allele the effect and frequency refer to;
chromosome spelling;
genome build.

It travels in the Release Bundle, checksummed, so resolution and Store Release Build read every file the same way. Today’s GWAS-SSF and FinnGen readers become built-in Column Maps. A dedicated reader remains only for a format a map cannot describe, such as GWAS-VCF or BESD.
Reformatting is acquisition’s job, done only when a map cannot cope. A structural change, such as splitting one file into one per Analysis, records in the Acquisition Manifest the original’s location and checksum and the tool that changed it. Nothing is built for this until a source needs it.
Clarified by #300: filtering to a release’s region policy at acquisition is a second, deliberate case, made for scale: download, filter, delete the original. It keeps the same lineage rule, and the lineage also records the region policy’s parameters. The QC-panel regions are always kept, so that Analysis Resolution can still measure ancestry and SD. The original is deleted only after the filtered file’s checksum is recorded. The filter is the registry’s (manifest_generation.region_filter) and may move upstream later; the policy is per release config (spec).
One historical exception is grandfathered: files whose originals were deleted before acquisition recorded lineage. Chen 2023’s 1,400 files (OGS-00006) were filtered by the retired R generator, which deleted each original and recorded its size but no checksum. Their lineage records the original’s location and size (original_bytes), with original_sha256 blank, and they carry the evidence R committed with the bundle (spec). No checksum is invented for them, and the exception covers no other file: every new acquisition records the original’s checksum.





Adapters as code the pipeline calls (fetch(analysis_ids)). This is a tighter interface, but it makes generation depend on live provider APIs. Two runs could then silently disagree, and every adapter would have to be written in the pipeline’s language.
One run per collection, routing each Analysis to a Store by Assigned Ancestry. This saves runs. But it re-homes a cohort whose frequencies look admixed, a scientific judgement that would be made silently by routing rather than shown as a check result.
A declared-only path for formats the resolver cannot read. It would let eQTLGen move now. But it creates a category with no Quality Checks, and it invites a release to declare values “just this once”.
A dedicated reader, or a conversion to GWAS-SSF, per new format. This is how today’s sources work, and it scales with the number of formats. The shared tabular core in OpenGWASDB already reduces the GWAS-SSF and FinnGen readers to column declarations; the Column Map makes that declaration data.
Resolution Records per Store Release. They would be re-measured for every Trial Store Release, every full release and every composition split, and two Stores could carry different measurements of one Analysis.





The package (#249) is step 0. The shared code moves into its final home before being reshaped.
Sources move onto the pipeline in this order:

GWAS Catalog first. It generalises candidate_workflow, and Chen, Sun and later GWAS Catalog collections then need only a release config.
FinnGen.
ukb-b, after the 2.5k OGS-00009 lands from its current generator.
dbGaP MVP.
eQTLGen, once OpenGWASDB resolves BESD.

Each move regenerates that source’s latest bundle and explains every difference from the committed one. Built and accepted bundles are never touched, and their recorded commands remain as history.
The R generators and their libraries retire as their sources move. This ends the duplicate ancestry and effect-scale code that contradicts ADR 0017.
OpenGWASDB owns two prerequisites: the Column Map reader and BESD resolution. The Column Map reader blocks no current source, because each one has a reader today. When it lands, MVP’s acquisition can stop rewriting dbGaP files into EBI’s GWAS-SSF.
The Release Bundle contract grows a Column Map for tabular collections, and per-Analysis Quality Check results.
ADR 0032’s decisions all stand. The thin workflow it describes becomes the pipeline every source uses. ADR 0009’s reader capability gains the Column Map.
crumbs: Manifest Generation is one pipeline fed by source connectors

No checksum is invented for them, and the exception covers no other file: every new acquisition records the original’s checksum.
crumbs: Manifest Generation is one pipeline fed by source connectors

title: Manifest Generation is one pipeline fed by source connectors
text:
Adapters as code the pipeline calls (fetch(analysis_ids)). This is a tighter interface, but it makes generation depend on live provider APIs. Two runs could then silently disagree, and every adapter would have to be written in the pipeline’s language.
One run per collection, routing each Analysis to a Store by Assigned Ancestry. This saves runs. But it re-homes a cohort whose frequencies look admixed, a scientific judgement that would be made silently by routing rather than shown as a check result.
A declared-only path for formats the resolver cannot read. It would let eQTLGen move now. But it creates a category with no Quality Checks, and it invites a release to declare values “just this once”.
A dedicated reader, or a conversion to GWAS-SSF, per new format. This is how today’s sources work, and it scales with the number of formats. The shared tabular core in OpenGWASDB already reduces the GWAS-SSF and FinnGen readers to column declarations; the Column Map makes that declaration data.
Resolution Records per Store Release. They would be re-measured for every Trial Store Release, every full release and every composition split, and two Stores could carry different measurements of one Analysis.
crumbs: Manifest Generation is one pipeline fed by source connectors

title: Manifest Generation is one pipeline fed by source connectors
text:
The package (#249) is step 0. The shared code moves into its final home before being reshaped.
Sources move onto the pipeline in this order:

GWAS Catalog first. It generalises candidate_workflow, and Chen, Sun and later GWAS Catalog collections then need only a release config.
FinnGen.
ukb-b, after the 2.5k OGS-00009 lands from its current generator.
dbGaP MVP.
eQTLGen, once OpenGWASDB resolves BESD.

Each move regenerates that source’s latest bundle and explains every difference from the committed one. Built and accepted bundles are never touched, and their recorded commands remain as history.
The R generators and their libraries retire as their sources move. This ends the duplicate ancestry and effect-scale code that contradicts ADR 0017.
OpenGWASDB owns two prerequisites: the Column Map reader and BESD resolution. The Column Map reader blocks no current source, because each one has a reader today. When it lands, MVP’s acquisition can stop rewriting dbGaP files into EBI’s GWAS-SSF.
The Release Bundle contract grows a Column Map for tabular collections, and per-Analysis Quality Check results.
ADR 0032’s decisions all stand. The thin workflow it describes becomes the pipeline every source uses. ADR 0009’s reader capability gains the Column Map.

title: Indexed Variant Subsets are optional, declared in the Build Recipe
text:
Epic opengwas/opengwasdb-stores#214 turns the HapMap3 extraction experiment (opengwas/opengwasdb#262, implemented in #263/#269) into routine release infrastructure. opengwas/opengwasdb ADR 0061 defines a named Indexed Variant Subset as an optional, rebuildable Dense-store query index over a caller-supplied list of canonical ALIDs, built by:
opengwasdb build-indexed-subset STORE SUBSET_NAME \
  --variant-list hm3.alid.txt --reference-assembly GRCh38
It is a non-authoritative derived artifact stored under data.zarr/indexed_subsets/<name>/; removing it leaves a valid release. A Compact release has no Dense Component, so it gets no subset. A Hybrid release’s subset lives on its self-contained Dense Component.
This registry must plan and run that step for a release that declares it. The capability first ships in opengwas/opengwasdb 4819a2ee (opengwas/opengwasdb #264), which is a descendant of the format-0.2.0 builders (opengwas/opengwasdb #240). The repository pin (7b0c42d) deliberately predates both, and adopting format 0.2.0 catalogue-wide is the separate migration tracked by stores#197.


A Build Recipe may declare one or more optional named subsets in a top-level indexed_subsets list:
indexed_subsets:
  - name: hm3
    resource_id: hapmap3-hg38
    variant_list: /data/opengwasdb/reference/hapmap3-hg38/hm3.grch38.alid.txt
    reference_assembly: GRCh38
    checksum: 4a7c82aa625a006ff437dcaa2769b00e056413d54c72e98f7378327c69513398
    options: {band-cells: 65536000}

name (required) is the subset identity, using the consumer’s own [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127} grammar and additionally refusing ...
resource_id, variant_list and reference_assembly (required) name the maintained variant-list Reference Resource (stores#208) and the concrete path and assembly the build uses. Recording the resolved path keeps the immutable bundle self-contained, and plan() needs no resource I/O.
checksum (optional) is the maintained list’s sha256, cross-checked against the resource declaration at run time.
options (optional) is opengwasdb flag passthrough for the subset command; overwrite is refused because a release declares a named subset to build, and so is any key that normalises to variant-list or reference-assembly, since those are the declaration’s own verified inputs and re-specifying one would let the executed CLI use a value the runtime never checked. The key is optional; omitting it declares none, while an explicit indexed_subsets: null is malformed rather than silently treated as omitted.

plan() emits one build-indexed-subset Step per declaration, in declaration order, after the Store and its inline top-hit/rho steps exist and before overview and validate, so overview reports the subset and validation audits it. The Step is an ordinary Step, so its durable records/indexed-subset-<name> .json carries planned and executed argv, inputs, outputs, stdout/stderr, timing, success and the opengwasdb revision used, with no new record schema. register already requires a record for every planned Step and compares executed against planned argv.
A Ragged release rejects an indexed_subsets declaration at plan time and in bundle.check(). It is never silently ignored: the epic’s non-goal is that Ragged releases get no HM3 subset, and CONTRIBUTING’s first rule is to fail loudly rather than skip a declaration. A recipe with no declaration, or an empty list, plans byte-for-byte as before.



The capability is a run-time prerequisite, not a tracked dependency change. Before a run that declares a subset, ogstores.release (and the Snakefile onstart hook, for a direct snakemake run) probes the resolved opengwasdb for build-indexed-subset and refuses with the required capability if it is absent. It also resolves the declaration’s resource_id under resources/reference-resources/<id>/resource.yaml and hashes the list against the maintained sha256, byte size and row count. plan() stays pure: it only renders argv.
This has two honest consequences:

A subset-declaring release runs the whole workflow on a capability runtime, because validate/overview must audit and report the namespace and because no opengwasdb revision has the subset feature without the format 0.2.0 builders. That release is therefore format 0.2.0 and its Validation Record names the actual runtime commit, not the tracked pin. This is opt-in per release; no existing 0.1.0 Store is touched and there is no bulk migration.
The pinned opengwasdb stays 7b0c42d until stores#197. A run that declares no subset is never gated on the runtime version, so every existing recipe and every no-declaration plan is unaffected.




stores#218 adopted the runtime portion of stores#197: the tracked pin is now 4e922566d7fa4c13a11be3637069da63e48be28c (core dev, repinned from the initial #218 pin 1be2a15 when core #254 merged). It carries the format-0.2.0 builders, the required Ragged/Overflow by_variant/ index, the Indexed Variant Subset capability and the shared HM3 benchmark seam. The decision above that the subset capability is an opt-in run-time prerequisite still holds, and the pre-run probe and resource hashing still run unchanged; what changes is consequence 2: the pinned runtime now provides the capability, so no PATH overlay is needed and a supported run never substitutes one. See docs/runtime.md.
The guard was generalized with the pin. ogstores.runtime.verify_runtime_for_releases now also refuses a run whose resolved executable’s identity is unprovable or is a revision other than the pin, whose scheduled steps name a subcommand the runtime lacks, or which would complete an existing parent Store that is not format 0.2.0. The parent gate is scheduled-step-aware: it applies only when the child’s own complete job will run, skips a stale parent when a same-run build/complete of that parent is scheduled, and refuses a missing parent that is not scheduled to be produced. Rejected option 3 above is superseded by this ticket: the format adoption is now deliberate and pinned rather than deferred, and it still does not convert, rebuild or requalify any published Store. A format-0.1.0 parent is refused and must be converted or rebuilt before Reference Completion, following the documented procedure in docs/runtime.md rather than an ad-hoc script contract.




Resolve the resource inside plan(). Rejected: plan() is a pure function with an executable tripwire test; opening resource.yaml or the list would break the planner contract the golden-argv suite protects. Resolution and hashing live in the run-time preflight instead.
Declare only resource_id and resolve it at plan time. Rejected for the same purity reason; recording the resolved path also keeps the immutable bundle self-contained and reviewable.
Bump the pin in this ticket. Rejected: every subset-capable revision also changes the Store format to 0.2.0, so a pin bump would silently adopt stores#197’s catalogue-wide migration. That decision belongs to #197.
Silently ignore a Ragged declaration. Rejected: a declared subset that is not built is a wrong answer that looks like a right one.
A separate subset index store. Rejected by opengwasdb ADR 0061: the index is a derived artifact under the release it accelerates.

title: Phase B candidate generation invokes the OpenGWASDB resolver
text:
Implements the first concrete Phase B Manifest Generator for the EBI GWAS Catalog hybrid__European release (issue #153), on the boundary ADR 0012, ADR 0017 and ADR 0023 already fixed.
Acquisition had produced a ~1.8 TB mirror and a frozen Source Inventory (issue #151); the ancestry and reference-AF policy decisions were settled in issue #152. What remained was the workflow that turns those into a candidate Release Bundle without building a Store and without re-implementing statistics OpenGWASDB already owns.
Amended by 0036. The workflow described here becomes the pipeline every Source Collection uses: its candidate table becomes a canonical Source Metadata Table, its freeze reconciles that table against an Acquisition Manifest for one Selection, and its exclusions become Quality Checks. Every decision below stands.
Amended by #284. The resolver’s checkpoint is no longer the Store Release’s own: it is shared per Source Collection, in the Resolution Area, and every run reuses each record whose fingerprint still matches. Accounting at emit therefore moves to the resolution receipt, which names each Analysis’s kept Resolution Record by fingerprint digest and checksum and refuses a record outside the Selection; an extra record in the shared checkpoint is another Selection’s, not a failure. The receipt-and-contract check below stands.


Expose one thin registry-owned candidate workflow that invokes opengwasdb resolve-analyses. The entry point is resources/generators/gwas-catalog-eur-hybrid/generate_candidate.py, run as pixi run generate-candidate OGS-xxxxx --config <config> --cores N [--resume]. It runs five stages — preflight, prepare, resolve, verify, emit — and workflow/generate.smk wires them as an optional coarse DAG.

The resolver owns the statistics and the durable work. opengwasdb resolve-analyses (opengwasdb#208) loads the genome-scale ancestry reference once, owns the process pool, and writes atomic, fingerprint-aware per-Analysis records with --resume. The registry never loads a reference, forks a worker, computes an ancestry, aligns an allele, or estimates a phenotype SD. That is ADR 0012’s “orchestration only” applied literally; the upstream commit is pinned by immutable revision in pixi.toml rather than vendored (ADR 0023).
The registry owns membership and the acceptance policy. From the frozen inventory’s exact data_file paths and the config’s defaults.by_study_design tiers it derives the canonical resolver manifest, and from the records it decides membership: which Analyses are in the candidate, which are exclude_from_build audit rows, and why. The controlled exclusion vocabulary is resolution_failed, ancestry_unassigned, ancestry_not_eur, orientation_failure, sd_no_reference_resource_for_ancestry, sd_no_qualifying_evidence, sd_no_usable_sample_size, sd_failed, missing_sample_size, missing_case_control_counts, no_build_eligible_rows, effect_placeholder_rows and not_maf_filtered (ADR 0033); each is explained in sidecars/exclusions.tsv.
Every record is accounted before anything is replaced. Finalisation refuses a selected Analysis with no record, a record that names an Analysis the manifest does not, a duplicate record, a record declaring an incompatible record_schema_version, or a record whose source identity, source file or method tier no longer matches the manifest resolved. The fingerprint digest is recomputed over the record’s own inputs.
A resolution receipt closes the stale-record hole a self-digest cannot. A record’s own fingerprint digest only proves it is internally consistent: a record produced under different gates, ancestry reference or fine-group map, extraction panel, reference-AF resources or tool revision still recomputes a valid self-digest. After a successful resolver invocation the workflow therefore atomically writes resolver/resolution_receipt.json, binding the resolver manifest’s checksum, the registry-recomputable slice of the resolution contract (declared gates, MAF floor, reader capability, extraction panel, ancestry reference/group-map and reference-AF resource content fingerprints), the installed resolver’s content identity, and every analysis_id to the fingerprint digest the resolver wrote for it. Standalone verify/emit recompute the contract from the current config, references and installed tool and require it to equal the receipt, and require every record digest to match the receipt. The registry never re-derives the resolver’s statistics; it binds and re-checks the inputs that determine them. Core count and --resume are recorded as evidence but are deliberately not part of the contract, so neither changes the contract or the bundle tables/sidecars.
Output is a candidate only, published atomically. The bundle is written under a hidden staging sibling, checked with bundle.check() and the pinned OpenGWASDB Analysis schema, and renamed into stores/<id>/ with the previous candidate restored if the rename fails. The workflow never writes an accepted status and never invokes Phase A.
Resolved metadata is joined, not re-selected. The candidate table (src/manifest_generation/providers/gwas_catalog/ebi-studies.r’s output, already checksummed by the #151 freeze) supplies the labels, publication identity, total N and the case/control counts the schema requires for log_or rows. Membership remains the frozen inventory’s; the join cannot add or drop a member.





release.yaml records the operator invocation and the exact opengwasdb resolve-analyses argv in generator.commands, plus the frozen inventory checksum and the preflight report path, so a reviewer can reproduce the candidate’s provenance.
analyses.tsv contains included rows and the exclude_from_build audit rows, honouring ADR 0025: bundle.check() and Phase A’s derived build manifest both drop the excluded rows, and the reason stays reviewable.
Aggregation is ordered by the frozen inventory and sidecar numerics go through the issue-#143 formatter, so 1 worker and 64 workers produce byte-identical tables and sidecars, and a resumed run reproduces an uninterrupted run’s bytes.
The resolution receipt is written after a successful resolve and is required by standalone verify/emit; a changed gate, reference, fine-group map, extraction panel, reference-AF resource or resolver revision makes it stale and forces a re-resolve rather than freezing stale Analyses into a candidate.
The Hybrid Build Recipe’s Dense-Component axis (--variant-reference / --reference-panel) is deliberately not declared in config-full.yaml: it is a Reference Resource decision for acceptance, and inventing a host path would bind the candidate to one machine. Acceptance adds one before the Store is built.
This does not change Phase A, which still consumes only the accepted bundle.

See store-release-workflow.md (Phase B), release-metadata-schema.md (sidecars), and the gwas-catalog-eur-hybrid README.

title: Artifact path is the identifier; the migration block is retired
text:
Amends the migration-note references in 0022 and the kept-field list in 0029.
The flat opaque Store id made a Store’s artifact path a pure function of its identifier: <artifact-root>/<store-id>/ (ADR 0022). In practice it was not: every Release Bundle carried a one-time migration block recording where the Store actually lived under the superseded family-first layout, and the indexer preferred that note when rendering store_uri, so the published master list pointed at legacy family-first paths in all seven rows. A one-time migration had become a permanent metadata tier.



The artifact path published in the master list (stores.tsv:store_uri) is a pure function of the identifier: <artifact-root>/<store-id>/store.opengwasdb, resolved from deployment configuration by paths.artifact_root() (issue #126) and never from a bundle field.
The migration-note fallback is removed from the indexer. render_stores_row no longer reads release.yaml:store_uri or release.yaml:migration.previous_store_uri.
The migration block is removed from every Release Bundle.
Store artifacts are not relocated in this ticket. Relocating the built Stores is hundreds of gigabytes of operational work and is out of scope for a registry change; it is raised as its own follow-up issue (#139), and this ticket records that dependency.





paths.py is the single module that constructs an artifact path, and store_path(store_id, root) is that pure function. Both renderings of the truth derive from it: plan() renders build_command (the Snakefile’s rules and the master list’s build_command column are one thing), and the indexer renders store_uri. They cannot disagree.
bundle.check() already rejects any artifacts block in a Build Recipe (issue #126), and there is no remaining bundle field that names an artifact location, so nothing can reintroduce a hand-maintained path into the master list.
The master list, every bundle’s summary.yaml, and both by-label/ trees are generated and verified in CI by regenerating and failing on a dirty tree, so a stale or hand-edited store_uri cannot quietly rot (ADR 0022’s “load-bearing master list” argument, now actually enforced for the artifact location).




The registry now publishes where a Store should live under the flat opaque-id layout. Whether a particular Trial Store Release’s bytes match that published location is an operational fact of the deployment it is running on, not a registry fact: the derived store_uri states the truth of the layout, and any on-disk mismatch is owned by the relocation follow-up issue, not a registry fact this column may silently re-encode.
This ADR originally stated the seven releases still sat at their legacy family-first paths. That blanket claim was itself wrong: re-verification on the production host (issue #142) found OGS-00001, OGS-00002, and OGS-00003 already present at <artifact-root>/<store-id>/store.opengwasdb with their legacy paths gone, and OGS-00004 through OGS-00007 at neither location there. Because the artifact root is deployment configuration (issue #126), this repository cannot verify every deployment, so the per-release, per-host state is recorded in stores/README.md rather than re-asserted here as a general truth.

The migration provenance block’s previous_store_uri was the last thing the indexer could read to prefer a legacy path over the identifier. title: Artifact path is the identifier; the migration block is retired
text:

title: Detached builds die with their orchestrator
text:
Detached builds die with their orchestrator
ogstores.run launches a release command with start_new_session=True so the command and every worker it forks share one signalable process group. That is what makes timeout, SIGINT, and nonzero-exit cleanup possible, but it also detaches the group from the orchestrator: if the process running execute_step is killed abruptly – Snakemake reaping a rule, a CI runner cancelling a job – no handler runs, the group keeps writing to store.opengwasdb.partial, and the next attempt collides with a build that is still in flight. Staging makes such a collision safe for the published Store but not for the retry.
The orchestrator therefore runs each command under a small supervisor that leads the isolated session (src/ogstores/_pdeath_supervisor.py) and holds the read end of a liveness pipe whose write end only the orchestrator holds and which is non-inheritable. When the orchestrator dies for any reason, including SIGKILL, the kernel closes the write end, the supervisor SIGKILLs the process group it leads, and nothing detached survives.
The supervisor does not own signal escalation. On timeout, SIGINT, or nonzero exit, _terminate_process_group keeps its existing two-phase contract – SIGTERM the group, wait out a grace window, then SIGKILL – and the supervisor’s handlers for SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP merely absorb the signal and keep waiting, so a command’s own SIGTERM handler runs to completion inside that window instead of being preempted by an immediate SIGKILL. Staying alive also keeps the supervisor’s stdio pipes open, so the orchestrator’s communicate() cannot return before the whole build is gone. Only the abrupt-parent-death path SIGKILLs, because no orchestrator remains to run the grace window.
Public behaviour and records are otherwise unchanged. The supervisor mirrors the command’s exit status, including death by signal (a SIGKILLed command still records -9), and reports a failed exec back through a one-shot exec-status pipe carrying the errno: ENOENT still becomes exit 127 / MissingCommandError, while EACCES or a directory still becomes exit 1 / StepExecutionError, exactly as the old direct Popen classified them.
The supervisor signals only a group it leads itself (os.getpgid(0) == os.getpid()). It never signals by pattern or by the parent’s group, so it cannot take out the orchestrator or a concurrent release in another worktree.
Three alternatives were considered and rejected:

Bare Linux PR_SET_PDEATHSIG. It reaches only the direct child, so opengwasdb’s forked ProcessPoolExecutor workers survive their leader’s death, which is exactly the collision being fixed. It also fires when the thread that called fork(2) exits, not only when the process dies, so a threaded orchestrator could lose a healthy build. The liveness pipe is process-scoped and needs no Linux-only interface.
Inherited locking. An exclusive lock held by the build group makes a retry fail fast instead of colliding, but it neither stops the orphan nor frees the artifact, so it does not satisfy “cannot leave the group alive”. It also adds a new failure mode to normal retries.
Pattern kills (pkill -f opengwasdb). Unsafe by construction: concurrent releases in other worktrees share the pattern.

Escape via a further setsid() still defeats group containment; that remains out of scope and requires external cgroup or container isolation, as the runner already documents.

title: One family record, and no Source Collection tier
text:
One family record, and no Source Collection tier
Amends 0009 and 0010.
Store Family records live in a single resources/families.yaml, one entry per family. The former families/<id>/family.yaml tree and the source-collections/ tree are both folded into it, and families/_candidates/ is retired.
A Store Family is a product identity, not a format. Three families in this registry are built from one Source Collection through one Source Format and one Source Reader Capability – gwas-catalog-eur-hybrid, metabolome-plasma-2023 and pqtl-interval-2018 are all EBI GWAS Catalog GWAS-SSF – and promise full-gwas, signals_only and cis_and_signals respectively. The format is what a builder sees; the family is what a query user sees, and a query user never learns the format. A family is also the unit of continuity across releases: ukb-b has four, and the promise has to survive all of them, which is why it cannot be a field restated on each one.
source_format is retired as a separate field. It and source_reader_capability were one fact written twice (finngen-r13-tabular / opengwasdb.finngen-r13), and only the capability is load-bearing because only it becomes an argument to an opengwasdb command. A null capability means the source is not read through the SourceReader registry at all – BESD, which build-ragged-besd reads directly – which the capability field expresses without a second field beside it.
The Source Collection stops being a directory and becomes a string. The tree recorded a provider, an access posture, a default licence, a format pair, an inventory and a status. The format pair is now one field; provider, posture and licence are inlined per family, and the licence is in any case already materialised per row in every analyses.tsv. The remaining two were inert: every collection declared inventory: null except one whose inventory.tsv was a header line with no rows, and all four declared status: candidate including those that had produced built Store Releases. No code ever read the directory – each generator took source_collection_id from its own configuration and copied it into release.yaml as a string.
Repeating provider, licence and capability across the three GWAS Catalog families is accepted deliberately. Three short fields in one file are cheaper to hold in the head, and easier to grep for drift, than a directory tier existing to normalise them.
ADR 0010’s rule that a Store Family is built from exactly one Source Collection now holds by construction rather than by inspection: the collection is a field on the family, so a family cannot name two.
A real Source Inventory would reopen this. When acquisition enumerates a collection at scale – the GWAS Catalog download is 2.35 TB across 17,300 files – the result cannot be a line in a YAML file. It returns as a data file, resources/inventories/<collection-id>.tsv, referenced from the family entry. That is a place to put rows, not a metadata tier, and it does not restore source-collections/.
A Candidate Store Family needs no home of its own. Its concrete expression is a candidate Store Release: stores/<id>/ with status: candidate, which the Release Status vocabulary already carries. What is under consideration and what has been built then appear in one generated master list. A proposal with no candidate release attached is a roadmap item and belongs in an issue tracker; families/_candidates/ held nothing but a README for the life of the repository.

Superseded by 0028. The Store Family record tier is deleted outright rather than folded further: every family field resolves to already-recorded, descriptive, or false on the evidence cited there; access_posture becomes a descriptive release.yaml field; and build priority moves to the issue tracker per this ADR’s own Candidate-Store-Family argument.

Amended by issue #134. Monolithic direct-read BESD releases (source_reader_capability: null, OGS-00001 and OGS-00002) currently record source identity only as an unverified host filesystem path prefix (source_snapshot.besd_prefix in OGS-00001; OGS-00002 carries only source_snapshot_id with lineage via derived_from) without checksums, file lists, or sizes, and bundle.check() only asserts that besd_prefix is a non-empty string for build-ragged-besd. This is a known integrity gap tracked by open issue #134, not an equivalent alternative to the checksum and source-identity verification enforced for per-Analysis formats.




 Back to top
crumbs: One family record, and no Source Collection tier

title: Flat opaque Store Release IDs
text:
Flat opaque Store Release IDs
Supersedes 0006 and 0018. Does not affect 0004, which governs when a new Store Release is required, not what it is called.
Every Store Release has one globally unique, opaque identifier of the form OGS- followed by five digits, allocated sequentially: OGS-00042. That identifier is the directory name in the registry (stores/OGS-00042/), the directory name under the artifact root (<artifact-root>/OGS-00042/), both the store_id and release_id written into an observed-only built store’s manifest, and the join key between the two. Reference Completion takes the child release_id while preserving its source Store identity under the upstream completion interface. The identifier is assigned once and never reused, reassigned, or re-derived.
Store Family stops being a directory level and becomes a field. A Store Family is an attribute of a Store Release — its query promise, access posture, release cadence, and build priority — and encoding an attribute in a path makes it unchangeable and unrepeatable. stores/OGS-00042/release.yaml carries family: finngen-r13, resolved against families/finngen-r13.yaml. The prior (Store Family ID, Family Release ID) pair is replaced by a single key, so no signature, path join, workflow wildcard, log line, or cross-family lineage link has to carry two strings to name one thing.
The identifier is opaque on purpose. Source-natural release names invite metadata to be stuffed into the identifier, where it cannot be validated and goes stale: this repository already carries dense-observed-vcf-c128-completed-issue34, which encodes source format, store layout, a zarr chunk size, completion state, and a GitHub issue number, all five of which are also recorded in build.yaml. An opaque identifier makes that impossible by construction, and it makes the generated master list (stores.tsv) the only way to find a release — so the master list is load-bearing rather than documentation, and cannot quietly rot.
Human legibility is restored by generated views rather than by identity. Every release carries a required label (the source-natural name that would previously have been its Family Release ID); tools display OGS-00042 (finngen-r13 / r13-pilot-20); and stores/by-label/ and <artifact-root>/by-label/ hold generated symlinks. Those views are derived and may be regenerated or discarded at any time. Nothing may resolve a release by label.
The label is descriptive provenance, not a replacement identity. The opengwasdb build CLI cannot currently populate it in the Store manifest’s free-form provenance mapping; upstream issue opengwasdb#181 tracks that capability. Until then it remains in the Release Bundle and generated views and is not placed in either manifest identity field.
Release Lineage is expressed once, as derived_from: OGS-00042 in the child’s release.yaml. The previous convention of naming a Reference-Completed child <parent>-completed expressed the same fact a second time through string adjacency; two mechanisms for one fact is how they drift apart. Because the artifact layout is now uniform, a store’s artifact path is a pure function of its identifier, so resolving a parent needs the identifier alone and never a registry lookup.
Existing published releases are renamed rather than preserved. This is a one-time mechanical migration of twenty bundles and their artifacts, recorded in the master list; the prior IDs remain discoverable through each release’s label and its migration note.

Amended by 0028. Store Family is no longer a field on a Store Release; the tier is retired entirely.
Amended by 0030. The one-time migration note recorded in each bundle is retired (issue #137): the published artifact path is now the pure function <artifact-root>/<store-id>/ with no migration fallback, and the physical relocation of existing artifacts is tracked by a separate follow-up issue.

Amended 2026-10-13 (owner-authorized renumbering). An identifier is still never silently reassigned, reused or re-derived. However, an explicit, owner-authorized renumbering is permitted when it is recorded end to end:

a durable owner decision naming the ordering;
an old→new mapping in the bundle’s migration block plus a notes erratum;
a matching physical directory rename (git mv), with the store_id updated;
association/index artifacts left byte-identical, and an evidence record.

The first case moved FinnGen from OGS-00016 to OGS-00017 so the MVP META observed-only Store could take OGS-00016 ahead of it (owner decision 2026-10-13, “reorder the IDs”); see docs/ogs-00016-to-ogs-00017-migration.md. The migration block is provenance for the renumbering only; store_uri remains a pure function of the identifier (ADR 0030).
Rejected alternatives:

Silent reassignment, or a directory rename alone. Rejected: the identifier is a join key across the registry, the artifact root and core-owned provenance; a rename without the recorded mapping, erratum and evidence is the silent rewrite this ADR forbids.
Reusing OGS-00016 for META without moving FinnGen. Rejected: it would collide with the existing artifact path and leave two releases claiming one identifier.
A permanent migration tier the indexer prefers. Rejected: store_uri stays identifier-derived; the block is never a path source.





 Back to top

title: Non-EUR LD Reference Panels are built from HGDP+1kGP, at structurally lower power
text:
Reference completion requires an ancestry-specific LD Reference Panel, so an Analysis can only be completed against a panel of its own Assigned Ancestry. Only EUR has one. It was generated on the UK Biobank RAP from 49,766 individuals at MAF ≥ 0.005 (MRCIEU/ukb-rap-utils, scripts/ld_matrix), and RAP access is not currently available — so the remaining ancestries cannot be produced the same way.
No locally available cohort comes close to that sample size. HGDP+1kGP offers roughly 500–1,000 individuals per super-population against UKB’s ~50,000. Because an LD matrix estimated from n individuals has rank at most n−1 regardless of how many variants it spans, and a typical block holds several thousand variants, non-EUR panels are not merely noisier than EUR — they are rank-deficient where EUR is full-rank. That gap cannot be closed by tuning: reaching p ≈ n would require ~800-variant blocks that would cut through real LD structure.


Build AFR, EAS and SAS LD Reference Panels from HGDP+1kGP (natively GRCh38, avoiding a liftover the EUR panel needed), and retain the existing UKB EUR panel for production rather than rebuilding it for cohort consistency. Discarding a 60×-better-powered panel to make the collection uniform would degrade the ancestry we have the most data for, to no analytical benefit.
Accept as a consequence that completion quality is permanently asymmetric across ancestries for reasons of panel construction rather than of the underlying GWAS. This asymmetry is made explicit in each panel’s Reference Resource declaration — source cohort, sample size, and variant-inclusion threshold — so it is legible to anyone comparing an AFR store against a EUR store.
Additionally build an HGDP+1kGP EUR panel as a calibration control, not for production. Holding ancestry fixed and varying only n is the only clean way to measure what the reduced sample size costs in imputation quality; without it, the usability of the non-EUR panels is a guess.
Parameters, recorded per panel rather than fixed by this decision:

Variant inclusion by minor-allele count (MAC ≥ 50), not minor-allele frequency. A frequency floor means different estimation precision in each panel as n varies; a count floor tracks precision directly and adapts across ancestries with differing sample sizes. The EUR panel’s MAF ≥ 0.005 gave ~500 copies; the same threshold at n ≈ 800 would give ~8, which is unestimable.
Existing ancestry-specific LD block definitions are reused (ld_regions_hg38.tsv), not recomputed. Block boundaries describe population recombination structure; re-deriving them from n ≈ 800 would produce noisier boundaries than those that exist, and would break comparability with the EUR panel that the calibration control depends on.
Variant identifiers are canonical store ALIDs (chr:pos:A1:A2), unlike the EUR panel’s chr:pos_ref_alt. The consuming code accepts both, but emitting ALIDs makes allele orientation unambiguous at rest rather than resolved at load, removing a class of failure where mis-parsed identifiers silently reduce imputation coverage.
Panel membership mirrors the ancestry-assignment super-populations, via an explicit recorded mapping parallel to the assignment’s own group map. Admixed populations (1kGP ASW, ACB) are excluded from AFR: recent admixture creates long-range LD absent from continental African populations, so including them would build a panel whose LD is wrong for exactly the Analyses routed to it.





Wait for UKB RAP access to be restored. Rejected as a blocker: the RAP pipeline already loops over AFR/EAS/SAS and would reuse unchanged, but UKB’s non-EUR counts (~8k SAS, ~8k AFR, ~2.5k EAS) are themselves far below EUR, so waiting buys a smaller improvement than it appears while blocking all non-EUR completion indefinitely.
Rebuild EUR from HGDP+1kGP for cohort consistency. Rejected: makes every panel equally weak rather than making the weak ones stronger, and sacrifices the ancestry with the most Analyses.
Extend to all seven assigned super-populations. Rejected: AMR, MID and NAF have no ancestry-specific LD block definitions, and HGDP+1kGP coverage of MID and NAF is thin. Analyses assigned to them remain observed-only, which Ancestry-Matched Completion already handles as a first-class state.
Collapse MID/NAF into adjacent panels. Rejected: that is precisely the admixture the fine-grained ancestry fit exists to detect, and it would impute against knowingly wrong LD rather than declining to impute.
Shrinkage LD estimation to regularise low-n matrices. Not adopted now: it is the standard remedy for small reference panels and would permit a lower MAC floor, but it changes the Reference Completion Method and its provenance contract. Retained as the escape hatch if calibration shows MAC-thresholding is insufficient.





Analyses assigned AMR, MID or NAF can be annotated and stored but never reference-completed, until block definitions and a panel exist for them.
Panel artifacts live outside this repository under the configured reference root and are referenced by resource_id, per the Registry-not-artifact-store rule.
The calibration control’s result determines whether the non-EUR panels ship at all, and should be recorded as release evidence rather than folklore.
Because completion quality now varies by panel provenance as well as by data quality, per-Analysis completion-quality summaries are the only reliable way to compare Analyses across ancestries.




The decision above left Analyses assigned AMR observed-only, because AMR had no block definitions. stores#241 measured an AMR calibration panel, and on 2026-10-22 the owner adopted a genome-wide one as the best AMR reference available until a better one exists. It is declared as hgdp1kgp-hg38-amr-ld rather than added to hgdp1kgp-hg38-ld, because three of its parameters differ from the AFR/EAS/SAS panels’.

Members. The 345 high-quality 1kGP Phase 3 AMR samples: CLM, MXL, PEL and PUR. HGDP’s American populations are excluded. They are small, bottlenecked, indigenous samples, not the admixed populations AMR-assigned Analyses come from. Pooling them would be a separate decision. As with ASW and ACB above, the panel’s LD is that of the populations it is built from.
Block layout. The EUR blocks, relabelled AMR, as in the EUR calibration control. LD is still estimated from AMR genotypes only. The pilot found more weak LD crossing EUR boundaries in AMR than in EUR. Imputation across an edge and AMR-derived boundaries remain untested.
Variant inclusion: MAF ≥ 0.01, not MAC ≥ 50. At n = 345 the MAC ≥ 50 floor above would be a 7.2% MAF filter, discarding about half the variants the pilot retained. The MAF floor is measured over called individuals, so it admits sparsely called sites. The panel therefore also requires at least 80% of members called, and FILTER PASS.
One record per ALID. gnomAD splits multi-allelic sites, so an insertion and a deletion at one position can share a canonical ALID (stores#348). Of the records that pass every filter, the one with the higher MAF is kept, and each block row records its source REF and ALT. The constructor now applies this to every panel it builds. The shipped AFR/EAS/SAS panels predate it and are tracked in stores#348.

The asymmetry this ADR accepts is widest here. At 345 individuals every block is capped at rank 344. In genotype-held-out calibration, masked z-scores were recovered with median r 0.85–0.92 outside the MHC, against 0.98–0.99 in-sample. That is not comparable with the EUR control’s real-GWAS 0.963 at n = 771. AMR completion quality is therefore lower than for any other ancestry, for reasons of panel construction, and the per-Analysis completion-quality summaries are the measure of it.
MID and NAF still have no panel and remain observed-only.

title: Non-EUR LD Reference Panels are built from HGDP+1kGP, at structurally lower power
text:
Build AFR, EAS and SAS LD Reference Panels from HGDP+1kGP (natively GRCh38, avoiding a liftover the EUR panel needed), and retain the existing UKB EUR panel for production rather than rebuilding it for cohort consistency. Discarding a 60×-better-powered panel to make the collection uniform would degrade the ancestry we have the most data for, to no analytical benefit.
Accept as a consequence that completion quality is permanently asymmetric across ancestries for reasons of panel construction rather than of the underlying GWAS. This asymmetry is made explicit in each panel’s Reference Resource declaration — source cohort, sample size, and variant-inclusion threshold — so it is legible to anyone comparing an AFR store against a EUR store.
Additionally build an HGDP+1kGP EUR panel as a calibration control, not for production. Holding ancestry fixed and varying only n is the only clean way to measure what the reduced sample size costs in imputation quality; without it, the usability of the non-EUR panels is a guess.
Parameters, recorded per panel rather than fixed by this decision:

Variant inclusion by minor-allele count (MAC ≥ 50), not minor-allele frequency. A frequency floor means different estimation precision in each panel as n varies; a count floor tracks precision directly and adapts across ancestries with differing sample sizes. The EUR panel’s MAF ≥ 0.005 gave ~500 copies; the same threshold at n ≈ 800 would give ~8, which is unestimable.
Existing ancestry-specific LD block definitions are reused (ld_regions_hg38.tsv), not recomputed. Block boundaries describe population recombination structure; re-deriving them from n ≈ 800 would produce noisier boundaries than those that exist, and would break comparability with the EUR panel that the calibration control depends on.
Variant identifiers are canonical store ALIDs (chr:pos:A1:A2), unlike the EUR panel’s chr:pos_ref_alt. The consuming code accepts both, but emitting ALIDs makes allele orientation unambiguous at rest rather than resolved at load, removing a class of failure where mis-parsed identifiers silently reduce imputation coverage.
Panel membership mirrors the ancestry-assignment super-populations, via an explicit recorded mapping parallel to the assignment’s own group map. Admixed populations (1kGP ASW, ACB) are excluded from AFR: recent admixture creates long-range LD absent from continental African populations, so including them would build a panel whose LD is wrong for exactly the Analyses routed to it.

title: Non-EUR LD Reference Panels are built from HGDP+1kGP, at structurally lower power
text:
Wait for UKB RAP access to be restored. Rejected as a blocker: the RAP pipeline already loops over AFR/EAS/SAS and would reuse unchanged, but UKB’s non-EUR counts (~8k SAS, ~8k AFR, ~2.5k EAS) are themselves far below EUR, so waiting buys a smaller improvement than it appears while blocking all non-EUR completion indefinitely.
Rebuild EUR from HGDP+1kGP for cohort consistency. Rejected: makes every panel equally weak rather than making the weak ones stronger, and sacrifices the ancestry with the most Analyses.
Extend to all seven assigned super-populations. Rejected: AMR, MID and NAF have no ancestry-specific LD block definitions, and HGDP+1kGP coverage of MID and NAF is thin. Analyses assigned to them remain observed-only, which Ancestry-Matched Completion already handles as a first-class state.
Collapse MID/NAF into adjacent panels. Rejected: that is precisely the admixture the fine-grained ancestry fit exists to detect, and it would impute against knowingly wrong LD rather than declining to impute.
Shrinkage LD estimation to regularise low-n matrices. Not adopted now: it is the standard remedy for small reference panels and would permit a lower MAC floor, but it changes the Reference Completion Method and its provenance contract. Retained as the escape hatch if calibration shows MAC-thresholding is insufficient.

title: Non-EUR LD Reference Panels are built from HGDP+1kGP, at structurally lower power
text:
Analyses assigned AMR, MID or NAF can be annotated and stored but never reference-completed, until block definitions and a panel exist for them.
Panel artifacts live outside this repository under the configured reference root and are referenced by resource_id, per the Registry-not-artifact-store rule.
The calibration control’s result determines whether the non-EUR panels ship at all, and should be recorded as release evidence rather than folklore.
Because completion quality now varies by panel provenance as well as by data quality, per-Analysis completion-quality summaries are the only reliable way to compare Analyses across ancestries.

title: Non-EUR LD Reference Panels are built from HGDP+1kGP, at structurally lower power
